A pheromone is a chemical substance that one living creature produces and releases into its surroundings, which then causes a specific reaction — either a behaviour or a body change — in another creature of the same species.

Think of it as a chemical message sent from one individual to another. It's an invisible signal, carried through the air, water, or a surface, that the receiver picks up and responds to — often automatically and instinctively, without any conscious decision.
Breaking It Down Simply

Three things make a pheromone what it is:

  1. It is a chemical. Not a sound, not a gesture — a molecule, a substance with a specific structure.
  2. It travels between individuals. One creature makes it; another creature receives it. It works outside the body, between bodies. (This is what separates it from a hormone, which is a chemical that travels inside one body, from one organ to another.)
  3. It targets only the same species. A bee's pheromone affects other bees, not butterflies. A dog's pheromone affects other dogs, not cats. This specificity is one of the most important features of pheromones.
How Pheromones Are Detected

In most animals, pheromones are detected through smell or taste — more precisely, through special chemical-sensing organs. In insects, these are often located on the antennae. In many mammals, there is a specific structure inside the nose called the vomeronasal organ (also called Jacobson's organ) that is dedicated to picking up pheromone signals. The brain then processes this chemical information and triggers the appropriate response.

What makes this remarkable is how precise the response can be. The receiver doesn't think about what to do — the pheromone triggers a built-in, pre-wired reaction.
The Two Broad Types of Pheromone Effects

Pheromones don't all work the same way. They fall into two broad categories based on what they do to the receiver:

1. Releaser pheromones
These cause a fast, immediate behavioural response. The reaction happens quickly — within seconds or minutes. These are the most commonly discussed type.

2. Primer pheromones
These cause a slower, deeper change — not in behaviour right away, but in the receiver's physiology (the biological processes inside their body). These take more time, sometimes days or weeks, to produce their effect.
Types of Pheromones by Purpose

Within these two broad categories, pheromones serve many specific roles. Here are the main ones:

Sex pheromones (or reproductive pheromones)
Used to attract a mate. This is the most well-known use of pheromones. A classic example: female silkworm moths release a chemical called bombykol. A male moth can detect just a handful of molecules of this substance from several kilometres away, and he will immediately fly in the direction of the source to find the female. The signal is extraordinarily powerful and precise.

Alarm pheromones
Released when an animal is threatened or injured, to warn others of danger. For example, when a bee stings an intruder, it releases an alarm pheromone that signals nearby bees to become defensive and join the attack. Similarly, when an ant is crushed or threatened, it releases chemicals that cause nearby ants to become aggressive or to scatter. These are releaser pheromones — the reaction is immediate.

Trail pheromones
Used by social insects, especially ants, to mark a path. When a worker ant finds a food source, it lays down a chemical trail on the ground as it walks back to the colony. Other ants follow this trail to the food. As more ants use the trail and reinforce it with their own pheromones, the signal grows stronger. When the food runs out, no new pheromone is laid, the trail fades, and ants stop following it. It is a beautifully self-regulating system.

Territorial pheromones
Used to mark an area as belonging to a particular individual or group, warning others to stay away. Many mammals do this — dogs and wolves urinate to mark territory, and the urine contains chemical compounds that communicate information to others of the same species: who was here, their sex, their reproductive status, how recently they passed through.

Aggregation pheromones
These attract members of the same species to gather in one location — for feeding, mating, or protection in numbers. Certain beetles, for instance, release these chemicals to bring large numbers of their species together on a tree.

Queen substance / dominance pheromones
This is a prime example of a primer pheromone. In a honeybee colony, the queen releases a complex mix of chemicals (called queen mandibular pheromone) continuously. This pheromone suppresses the reproductive development of all the worker bees — they are biologically capable of reproducing, but the queen's pheromone keeps that ability switched off. It also prevents worker bees from raising new queens. The entire social structure and order of the colony is maintained partly through this invisible chemical signal. When the queen dies and the pheromone disappears, the workers begin to raise new queens within hours — showing just how powerful this chemical control is.
Which Animals Use Pheromones?

Pheromones are used across an enormous range of life:

  • Insects — the most extensively studied group. Ants, bees, wasps, moths, butterflies, beetles, and cockroaches all rely heavily on pheromones.
  • Fish — many fish species release pheromones into the water to signal reproductive readiness.
  • Amphibians and reptiles — frogs and salamanders use chemical signals for mating; many snakes sense pheromones through their tongues and the Jacobson's organ in the roof of their mouth.
  • Mammals — dogs, cats, mice, rabbits, deer, elephants, and many others use pheromones for mating signals, territory marking, mother-infant bonding, and group cohesion.
What About Humans?

This is a genuinely fascinating and still somewhat open question. Humans do have traces of the vomeronasal organ, but in adults it appears to be non-functional or vestigial (a remnant of something that worked better in our evolutionary past). The scientific community largely agrees that humans do not use pheromones in the same clear, direct, automatic way that insects or most other mammals do.

However, there is evidence of some chemical communication in humans. Newborn babies appear to locate their mother's nipple by smell alone, and mothers can often identify their own baby by scent. Some studies suggest that women's mate preferences are subtly influenced by the body odour of men with different immune system genetics (the MHC or HLA system). But whether these effects qualify as true pheromone responses — with specific chemicals causing specific automatic reactions — is still debated. What's certain is that if human pheromones exist, they are far more subtle and less clear-cut than in other animals.
Pheromones vs. Hormones — The Key Distinction

This is worth cementing clearly, because people sometimes confuse the two:

HormonePheromone
Where it travelsInside one bodyBetween two bodies
Who it affectsThe same individual that produced itA different individual of the same species
ExampleAdrenaline makes your heart beat fasterAn alarm pheromone makes another ant flee

Both are chemical signals. Both trigger specific responses. But a hormone is an internal messenger, while a pheromone is an external messenger between individuals.
Pheromones in Human Use

Because pheromones trigger such specific, predictable responses, humans have found practical ways to use them:

  • Pest control: Synthetic sex pheromones of agricultural pests (like moths) are used in traps to lure and capture males, disrupting their mating and reducing crop damage — without using toxic pesticides.
  • Research and veterinary science: Synthetic pheromones are used to calm anxious dogs and cats (commercial products like "Adaptil" for dogs and "Feliway" for cats mimic natural calming pheromones).
  • Conservation: Pheromone traps help scientists monitor insect population levels in forests to predict and prevent infestations.
In Summary

A pheromone is a chemical signal produced by one organism that travels through the environment and triggers a specific, often automatic response — behavioural or physiological — in another member of the same species. It is nature's chemical language: precise, powerful, and operating mostly below the level of conscious awareness. It is distinct from a hormone in that it works between individuals rather than within a single body. Pheromones are central to how insects organise their colonies, how animals find mates, how territory is marked, and how creatures warn each other of danger — making them one of the oldest and most fundamental forms of communication in the living world.
